summary: For ages 9-10, real-world maths modelling means running the full cycle — choose a representation that fits the situation's structure, build it, compute, then interpret the result back in the right units with a plausibility check. At this age the new skill is SELECTING among competing models (percentage bar, scale diagram, double number line/ratio table, area rectangle) rather than being handed one. The recurring failure is answering with a by-product of the calculation (the discount £10, or the proportion 0.75) rather than the quantity the situation actually asked for (the £30 a shopper pays), and never sense-checking (a sale price must be below the original).
misconceptions: Gives the discount amount (£10 off) when asked the sale price (£30), or leaves the answer as a decimal (0.75) never returned to pounds
Confuses area and perimeter — adds sides when the situation needs area, or reports the carpet answer in cm instead of cm²
Applies a percentage as a raw number ('25% is 25') rather than a proportion of the specific amount
Picks a representation by habit rather than fit, so a rate problem gets a single bar that hides the two varying quantities
Scales additively (adds the same amount) instead of multiplicatively when enlarging a recipe or shape

activities.title: Choose, build, interpret back: a modelling workbench
steps: Take a situation such as 'a £40 jacket has 25% off — what does a shopper pay?' and first choose which representation exposes its structure from a palette: percentage bar, scale diagram, double number line, or ratio table
Build a percentage bar: partition the 100% strip into quarters, shade off one quarter (the discount), and read what remains
State explicitly what each number refers to: £10 is the discount (25% of £40), 0.75 is the proportion of the original price remaining, and £30 is the price paid
Pass an interpret-back gate: state the final answer with its unit (£30) and check it is reasonable — a sale price must be less than £40

Re-run the same process on a room-carpet problem (choose a scale diagram, apply the area formula, and give the area in a squared unit that matches the length unit of the measurements — e.g. a 4 m × 3 m room needs 12 m² of carpet) and a recipe-scaling problem (choose a double number line, answer in grams)
Notice which representation you reach for — if you grab a single bar for a rate problem that has two varying quantities, ask whether it hides structure
activities.insight: When the question asks what the shopper pays, the answer is the part that STAYS (£30), not the part taken off (£10) nor the bare proportion (0.75); and a model is chosen to fit a situation's structure, with every answer returned to its real units and sense-checked.

activities.title: Defend the answer to a customer or tradesperson
steps: Work in role with a customer or decorator who only accepts an answer once it is stated as the real quantity they need
Answer the shopkeeper's probe 'you said 30 — is that the discount or what I pay?' by distinguishing the two
Answer the decorator's probe 'is that enough for a 4 m by 3 m room?' by stating an area with its unit (12 m²) and checking it is plausible
Voice the reasonableness check aloud: '£30 — less than £40, so for a sale it makes sense'
activities.insight: The reflective close of the modelling cycle can be spoken: you name which number is the discount, which is the proportion, and which is the quantity asked for, and you justify that it is sensible.

activities.title: Feel area as coverage, length as edge (optional spatial scaffold)
steps: Cover the floor of a room to feel area as coverage, reported in a squared unit matching the measurements (e.g. m² of carpet needed for a metre-dimensioned room)
Measure around the edge of the same floor to feel length, reported as a length matching the measurements (e.g. m of skirting or edging)
Say out loud which quantity a given question asks for before computing, and match the unit to it
activities.insight: Area (coverage) and perimeter (edge length) are physically different quantities with different units; blurring them is the error, not a detail.

checkQuestion: A £40 jacket has 25% off. A shopper says the answer is 10. Another says it's 0.75. What has each of them worked out, and what is the price the shopper actually pays? How would you know your final answer is sensible?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child distinguishing that '10' is the discount (25% of £40) and '0.75' is the fraction/proportion remaining, and that the price PAID is £30; and for a reasonableness check ('£30 is less than £40, which must be true for a sale'). A child who cannot say what 10 and 0.75 each refer to, or who names one of them as the price, is computing without modelling.
